lessons.title: Setting Up a Street Kitchen
lessons.body: Start with a spot that has three things: foot traffic, shade, and a water source within 50 metres. In most African cities, you need a permit from the local council. Visit the municipal offices and ask for the 'hawker's licence' or 'street trading permit'. In Nairobi, it costs about 2,000 KES per year; in Accra, around 100 GHS per quarter. Budget for it. Your stall must be stable. Use a wooden table at least 1 metre long and 70 cm high. If you fry, place your oil drum or gas cooker on a separate metal stand, never on the same table where you chop vegetables. Keep a 2-metre gap between the cooking fire and where customers stand. For storage, use two plastic crates with lids: one for dry goods (flour, salt, spices), one for tools (knives, spoons, tongs). Never store food on the ground. A simple three-sided windbreak made from corrugated iron sheets will protect your flame and keep dust off your food. For washing, bring two 20-litre jerrycans: one with clean water and soap, one for rinsing. A small basin and a bottle of liquid soap cost less than 500 KES. Set up a handwashing station at the front of your stall so customers see you wash. Finally, arrange your workspace in a line: raw ingredients on the left, cooking in the centre, finished food and serving on the right. This prevents cross-contamination and speeds up service. Test your setup at home before you go live. Time yourself: you should be able to serve your first customer within 15 minutes of arriving.

lessons.title: Charcoal, Gas and Wood: Choosing Your Heat
lessons.body: Charcoal is the most common street fuel in Africa because it is cheap, widely available, and gives high heat. A 50 kg sack of charcoal in Kampala costs about 80,000 UGX and lasts 5-7 days if you cook 6 hours a day. Charcoal burns at 600-800Â°C, perfect for deep frying and grilling. But it produces carbon monoxide, so never use it in a closed room. Gas (LPG) is cleaner and faster to control. A 6 kg cylinder costs around 15,000 NGN in Lagos and lasts 10-12 days if you fry 4 hours daily. Gas burns at 1,000Â°C and you can turn it off instantly, saving fuel. However, refilling can be unreliable in rural areas. Wood is free in many villages but burns slower and produces more smoke. Use dry hardwood, not softwood, to avoid creosote that flavours food badly. For a beginner, start with charcoal: it is forgiving and you can see the heat. Buy a 'jiko' (Kenya) or 'coal pot' (Ghana) for 500-1,500 KES. For gas, buy a single-burner stove with a hose and regulator. Always check the hose for cracks before lighting. For wood, build a three-stone fire and keep a bucket of sand nearby to control flames. Whichever you choose, never leave a fire unattended. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry powder, 1 kg) or a bucket of sand within arm's reach. Learn to judge heat by holding your palm 15 cm above the coals: if you can hold it for 3 seconds, it is medium; 1 second, high. This skill saves fuel and prevents burnt food.

lessons.title: Oil for Frying: Types, Temperature, Reuse
lessons.body: Use vegetable oils with a high smoke point: palm oil (smoke point 235Â°C), groundnut oil (225Â°C), sunflower oil (225Â°C), or canola (205Â°C). Avoid olive oil for deep fryingâit is expensive and smokes at 190Â°C. In West Africa, red palm oil gives colour and flavour to puff-puff and plantain, but it foams. Let it settle for 10 minutes after heating before frying. In East Africa, sunflower oil is common and cheap. Buy in 5-litre jerrycans to save money: 5 litres of sunflower oil in Dar es Salaam costs about 25,000 TZS. Heat oil to 170-180Â°C for most doughnuts and fritters. If you don't have a thermometer, drop a 1 cm cube of bread: it should brown in 60 seconds. If it browns in 30 seconds, the oil is too hot (200Â°C+); if it takes 90 seconds, too cool. Reuse oil only 3-4 times. Each time, strain it through a fine mesh or cloth to remove crumbs. Store in a dark, cool place. When oil turns dark, smells rancid, or foams excessively, throw it away. Never mix old oil with new. To dispose, let it cool, pour into a sealed container, and give to a soap maker or waste collectorânever down the drain. For safety, keep a lid nearby to smother flames if oil catches fire. Never use water on an oil fire. A simple oil thermometer costs 5,000 KES and pays for itself in one week by preventing burnt batches.

lessons.title: The Dough Toolkit: Mixing, Resting, Shaping
lessons.body: You need five tools: a large bowl (plastic or stainless steel, 5-litre), a wooden spoon or your clean hands, a measuring cup, a clean cloth, and a flat surface for kneading. For most street doughsâmandazi, puff-puff, doughnutsâuse all-purpose flour. In Nigeria, you might use cassava flour for 'akara' but that's a batter, not a dough. Start with a basic ratio: 500 g flour, 1 teaspoon instant yeast, 1 teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons sugar, 250 ml warm water (not hotâhot water kills yeast). Mix dry ingredients first. Add water slowly, stirring with a spoon until it forms a shaggy mass. Then knead on a floured surface for 8-10 minutes until smooth and elastic. If it sticks, add flour one tablespoon at a time. Resting is critical: cover with a damp cloth and leave in a warm place for 1-2 hours until doubled in size. In cold weather, put the bowl near your fire but not too close. After resting, punch down the dough to release air. Shape into balls (50 g each for mandazi) or rings. For puff-puff, use a spoon to drop small balls into oil. Always shape with clean, oiled hands to prevent sticking. If you want to save time, make the dough the night before and keep it in a cool box with ice packs. It will rise slowly and be ready by morning. Never skip restingâit makes the dough light and digestible. Test a small piece first: fry one ball. If it floats and browns in 2 minutes, your oil is ready.

lessons.title: Food Safety on the Street
lessons.body: Street food must be safe or you will lose customers and get sick yourself. The biggest risks are bacteria from raw meat, dirty water, and dirty hands. Keep raw meat and vegetables separate. Use two cutting boards: red for meat, green for vegetables. If you can't afford two, cut vegetables first, then meat, then wash the board with soap and hot water. Cook meat to 75Â°Câno pink inside. For fried foods, oil at 175Â°C kills most bacteria in 2 minutes. Never leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours. If you prepare ahead, keep hot food above 60Â°C and cold food below 5Â°C. In hot African climates, bacteria double every 20 minutes. So serve immediately or reheat thoroughly. Cover all food with mesh lids or clean cloths to keep flies off. Flies carry typhoid and cholera. Buy a fly trap or use a fan to create a breeze. Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds after using the toilet, handling raw meat, or touching money. Keep a bottle of hand sanitiser (70% alcohol) for quick clean-ups. Never smoke or chew while cooking. Wear a clean apron and tie back long hair. If you have diarrhoea or a cut on your hand, stay home or wear gloves. Clean your stall at the end of each day: scrape tables, sweep the ground, and wash utensils in hot soapy water. A clean stall attracts more customersâthey can see you care.

lessons.title: Water, Cleanliness and Hand Hygiene
lessons.body: Water is the most common source of sickness in street food. Never use tap water directly unless you know it is treated. In most African cities, tap water is chlorinated but may still contain bacteria. Boil water for 1 minute, then cool it in a clean covered container. Or use a filter (ceramic or biosand) or add 2 drops of household bleach (5% sodium hypochlorite) per litre, wait 30 minutes. For washing hands, use running waterânot a bowl where everyone dips. A simple 'tippy-tap' made from a 5-litre jerrycan with a hole and a string costs nothing and saves water. Fill it with clean water and hang it at your stall. Add soap. Wash hands for 20 seconds: palms, back of hands, between fingers, under nails. Rinse. Dry with a clean cloth or air dry. For washing utensils, use three basins: wash with soap and hot water, rinse with clean water, then sanitise with a bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres water) for 1 minute. Air dry on a clean rackâdo not wipe with a dirty cloth. For dishes, use a separate basin from handwashing. Change water every 2 hours or when it looks dirty. Store clean water in a covered container with a tap or ladleânever dip a cup into it. If you use a bucket, keep a dedicated scoop that only touches water. Finally, keep your fingernails short and clean. Dirt under nails carries bacteria. Wash your hands before you start cooking, after handling money, after using the toilet, and after touching your face or phone. A bar of soap and a jerrycan cost less than 500 KES but can save you from a week of sickness and lost sales.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Fire, Oil and Dough â The Street Kitchen Operator's Handbook

This Practical Reference consolidates the six lessons in Foundations: Fire, Oil and Dough into one working document. It is written for the operator who is already selling â or about to sell â fried dough, mandazi, puff-puff, vetkoek, kebab, chips, chapati or bhajia from a roadside stand, a market bay, a school gate or a mobile cart. Every decision here is framed around three business questions: Does it reduce my cost per unit? Does it protect my customer? Does it keep me trading tomorrow?

Street food in Africa is not a side hustle â it is a major employer and a daily food source for millions. The World Bank estimates that the food system employs a large share of the continent's workforce, and informal food vending is one of the most accessible entry points for women and youth entrepreneurs. Your margin comes from three controllable inputs: heat, oil and dough. Master these and you control your business.

1. Choice of Heat: Cost, Control and Compliance

Your heat source is a business decision, not just a cooking decision. Charcoal is cheap to start but variable in output; LPG is clean and controllable but requires cylinder purchase and refills; firewood is the cheapest but is banned or restricted in many urban centres because of smoke and deforestation. The table below compares the three options on the metrics that affect your daily profit.

Table 1. Heat source comparison for a typical street frying unit (approx. 30â60 meals/day)
Factor Charcoal LPG (gas) Firewood
Typical start-up cost Low (brazier + first bag) High (cylinder deposit + regulator) Very low
Temperature control Poor â needs constant tending Excellent â turn a knob Poor â smoky and uneven
Smoke / indoor use Moderate; needs ventilation Clean; safe indoors with ventilation High; often restricted by city by-laws
Health risk CO poisoning if enclosed Explosion if leaking; store upright Respiratory illness from smoke
Best for Grilling, low-volume frying High-volume consistent frying Rural / off-grid settings only

Sources: WHO Household air pollution and health fact sheet (2023); Global Alliance for Clean Cookstoves market assessments; national LPG promotion programmes (e.g. Kenya's Petroleum Institute, Nigeria's NLNG).

2. Oil: Temperature, Reuse and Cost Control

Oil is usually the single largest recurring cost in a fried-dough or chips business â often 15â25% of turnover. It is also the most common food safety failure point. Frying below 160 Â°C makes dough greasy and oil-logged; above 190 Â°C the oil breaks down quickly and forms acrylamide and other harmful compounds. The sweet spot for most African fried dough is 170â180 Â°C.

Table 2. Frying oil reference: smoke point, typical use and reuse limits
Oil type Smoke point Best use Practical reuse limit
Palm oil (red) ~230 Â°C Mandazi, puff-puff, plantain 3â5 fry sessions if filtered daily
Groundnut oil ~225 Â°C General frying, chips 3â4 sessions
Sunflower oil ~225 Â°C Chips, bhajia 2â3 sessions
Refined vegetable blend ~200â210 Â°C Budget option 2 sessions maximum
Used / re-refined oil Variable, often <180 Â°C Not recommended Do not use

Sources: FAO Fats and fatty acids in human nutrition (2010); WHO Healthy diet fact sheet (2020); Codex Alimentarius Code of Practice for the Prevention and Reduction of Acrylamide in Foods (CAC/RCP 67-2009).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Cooking oil fires and hot oil burns

Never throw water on a burning oil pan â it causes a violent steam explosion. Cover the pan with a metal lid or damp cloth, turn off the heat, and if safe, smother with sand or a dry-powder extinguisher. Keep a bucket of dry sand within arm's reach of every frying station. Never leave hot oil unattended, never fill a pan more than one-third full, and never let children or untrained helpers stand at the fryer. Hot oil at 180 Â°C causes full-thickness burns in under one second.

3. The Dough Toolkit: Consistency Is Profit

Dough is where your brand lives. A mandazi that is soft today and hard tomorrow loses customers. The four-step toolkit â mix, rest, shape, fry â should be standardised so that any trained helper produces the same result. Weigh ingredients rather than using cups; a 5% variation in water changes texture noticeably. Rest the dough covered for at least 30 minutes at ambient temperature (longer in cool highland areas, shorter in hot coastal towns) so the gluten relaxes and the dough shapes without shrinking. Shape on a lightly floured board, never on a wet surface. Fry in small batches â overcrowding drops the oil temperature below 160 Â°C and produces greasy, pale dough.

4. Food Safety on the Street: The Five Keys in Practice

The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food are the global standard: keep clean; separate raw and cooked; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials. On a street stand these translate into concrete actions: a tippy-tap or jerrycan with a tap for handwashing (not a shared bowl), a covered display so flies cannot land on cooked food, a clean cloth for drying hands (changed daily), and a separate pair of tongs for raw and cooked dough. If you handle money, wash hands or use a tong-and-cash-box system â cash is one of the dirtiest items on your stand.

5. Water, Cleanliness and Hand Hygiene

Water is both an ingredient and a cleaning input. Use potable water for dough and for rinsing utensils. Where piped water is unreliable, treat water by boiling (rolling boil for 1 minute) or by using an approved chlorine tablet. Hand hygiene is the single highest-return habit in street food: wash with soap for at least 20 seconds before starting, after handling raw dough, after using the toilet, after handling waste, and after touching money. Keep fingernails short, cover cuts with waterproof plasters, and wear a clean apron. The WHO estimates that handwashing with soap alone can reduce diarrhoeal disease by around 30% â a direct saving on lost trading days.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Heat: Set up burner on a stable, level surface away from customers and flammable materials; keep sand or extinguisher within reach.
  • Oil: Check temperature with a thermometer before the first batch â target 170â180 Â°C; never fry below 160 Â°C.
  • Oil reuse: Filter after each session, store in a covered tin away from sunlight, and discard when it darkens, foams or smells rancid.
  • Dough: Weigh ingredients, rest covered for at least 30 minutes, and fry in small batches to protect oil temperature.
  • Separation: Keep raw dough, cooked food and money physically apart â separate tongs, separate surfaces.
  • Hygiene: Tippy-tap with soap at the stand; wash hands for 20 seconds before, during and after handling food or cash.
  • Water: Use potable water for dough and rinsing; treat stored water by boiling or approved chlorine.
  • Display: Keep all cooked food covered; never display food on the ground or near a drain.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  1. WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (2006). who.int/publications
  2. FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â Code of Hygienic Practice for Street-Vended Foods (CAC/RCP 43-1997, Rev. 2011). fao.org/codexalimentarius
  3. FAO â Street Food Vending in Africa: Opportunities and Challenges (FAO publications portal). fao.org/publications
  4. WHO â Household Air Pollution and Health fact sheet (2023). who.int/fact-sheets
  5. Codex Alimentarius â Code of Practice for the Prevention and Reduction of Acrylamide in Foods (CAC/RCP 67-2009). fao.org/codexalimentarius

Bottom line: Control your heat, protect your oil, standardise your dough, and never compromise on hygiene. These four habits are the difference between a stall that closes in six months and a street food brand that employs your neighbours.

quiz.q: What is the minimum distance your cooking fire should be from where customers stand?
quiz.explanation: A 2-metre gap prevents burns and keeps customers safe.

quiz.q: Which document do you need from local council to legally trade on the street?
quiz.explanation: A hawker's licence or street trading permit is required in most African cities.

quiz.q: What is the approximate smoke point of palm oil?
quiz.explanation: Palm oil has a high smoke point of about 235Â°C, suitable for deep frying.

quiz.q: How many times can you safely reuse frying oil?
quiz.explanation: Reusing oil 3-4 times is safe if strained and stored properly; more leads to rancidity.

quiz.q: What should you do if your oil catches fire?
quiz.explanation: Covering with a lid smothers the fire; water spreads it.

quiz.q: What is the ideal water temperature for activating yeast in dough?
quiz.explanation: Warm water (40-46Â°C) activates yeast without killing it; boiling water kills it.

quiz.q: How long should you knead dough for mandazi or puff-puff?
quiz.explanation: Kneading for 8-10 minutes develops gluten, making dough smooth and elastic.

quiz.q: What is the minimum internal temperature for cooked meat to be safe?
quiz.explanation: 75Â°C kills most harmful bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food sit at room temperature before it becomes unsafe?
quiz.explanation: After 2 hours, bacteria multiply rapidly, especially in hot climates.

quiz.q: What is the correct bleach-to-water ratio for sanitising utensils?
options: A) 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres water
B) 1 cup bleach per 1 litre water
C) 1 teaspoon bleach per 10 litres water
D) 1 litre bleach per 1 litre water
quiz.explanation: 1 tablespoon of 5% bleach per 4 litres of water is a safe sanitising solution.

quiz.q: What is a 'tippy-tap' used for?
quiz.explanation: A tippy-tap is a simple jerrycan with a hole and string for hands-free handwashing.

quiz.q: Which fuel burns at the highest temperature?
quiz.explanation: LPG burns at around 1,000Â°C, higher than charcoal (600-800Â°C) or wood.

quiz.q: What is the recommended oil temperature for deep frying doughnuts?
quiz.explanation: 170-180Â°C is ideal for even cooking without burning the outside.

quiz.q: How can you test if oil is at the right temperature without a thermometer?
options: A) Drop a bread cube; it should brown in 60 seconds
B) Touch the oil with your finger
C) Wait for it to smoke
quiz.explanation: A bread cube browning in 60 seconds indicates roughly 175Â°C.

quiz.q: Why should you never store food on the ground?
options: B) It attracts pests and bacteria
quiz.explanation: Ground contact brings dirt, pests, and bacteria that cause illness.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for washing utensils?
quiz.explanation: Wash with soap, rinse clean, then sanitise with bleach solution.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
quiz.explanation: 20 seconds of scrubbing removes most germs.

quiz.q: What is the best way to dispose of used cooking oil?
options: C) Give to soap maker or waste collector
quiz.explanation: Recycling oil prevents clogged drains and environmental harm.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sign that frying oil should be discarded?
options: D) It is clear and golden
quiz.explanation: Clear, golden oil is still good; dark, rancid, or foamy oil should be thrown away.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of using charcoal in a closed room?
quiz.explanation: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can be fatal in enclosed spaces.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gap between your cooking fire and your serving table?
quiz.explanation: A 2-metre gap prevents cross-contamination and burns.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for shaping dough without sticking?
quiz.explanation: Oiling your hands prevents dough from sticking during shaping.

quiz.q: How long should you rest dough for it to double in size?
quiz.explanation: 1-2 hours in a warm place allows yeast to ferment and dough to rise.

quiz.q: What should you do before using a gas cylinder?
quiz.explanation: Cracked hoses leak gas and cause explosions; always inspect before lighting.

quiz.q: Which cutting board colour is typically used for raw meat?
quiz.explanation: Red boards are standard for raw meat to prevent cross-contamination.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time you should keep cooked food hot above 60Â°C?
quiz.explanation: After 2 hours, even hot food can grow bacteria if temperature drops.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep fingernails short and clean?
options: B) To prevent dirt and bacteria under nails
quiz.explanation: Dirt under nails harbours bacteria that can contaminate food.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store clean water for cooking?
options: B) In a covered container with a tap or ladle
quiz.explanation: Covered storage with a tap or dedicated ladle prevents recontamination.

quiz.q: How often should you change handwashing water at your stall?
options: A) Every 2 hours or when dirty
quiz.explanation: Dirty water spreads germs; change every 2 hours or when visibly soiled.

quiz.q: What is the best way to keep flies off your food?
options: A) Use mesh lids or clean cloths
quiz.explanation: Mesh lids and cloths create a physical barrier without chemicals.
